findings.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P1 confidence 100] The lifecycle ownership is split across incompatible feature selectors: `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` gates deletion cleanup while every factory at lines 40–68 selects `MgmtPermissionsV2` with `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, so a V2-only realm deleting a role, client, or group skips the state transition that removes its authorization associations and leaves derived permission data orphaned.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — [P1 confidence 100] Per-client resource identity is modeled inconsistently because `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())` queries owner `server.getId()` while `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` at `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` persists owner `resourceServer.getClientId()`, so evaluating any client-specific grant misses the instance resource, falls back to the aggregate `Clients` resource, and disconnects the grant from the client operation it is meant to authorize.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P1 confidence 100] Wrong-shape advisory: `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` assumes per-client resources carry type `Clients`, but creation at `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` never calls `setType`, so role-mapping discovery sees only the aggregate resource and emits its name `Clients` instead of domain client IDs, making the next instance-filtered client scope impossible to add until type and domain identity are explicit; the strongest counterargument is that each resource name already stores the client ID, but it does not survive because this path selects by type before reading the name.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P2 confidence 75] Once the missing instance type is corrected, `findByType(... resource -> { if (hasGrantedPermission(resource, scope)) ... })` performs a full unpaged resource scan, invokes `root.evaluatePermission` once per resource at line 276, and materializes every grant in a `HashSet`, so listing role mappings becomes an N+1 policy-evaluation path whose work and memory grow without the downstream page size; the strongest counterargument is that only permission-bearing clients create resources, but it does not survive because that set is unbounded and the API returns all IDs before pagination.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:207 — [P2 confidence 75] Simplification advisory: the duplicated `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, `hasPermission(String)`, and `hasGrantedPermission(Resource, String)` branches separately encode realm checks, resource selection, evaluation, and nested scope scans, so adding the next resource type or selector requires three synchronized edits and has already allowed owner/type drift; a typed resource-key evaluator would make the fallback branches at lines 215–222 and 245–247 plus the repeated scans at lines 225–232, 250–257, and 277–283 unnecessary, and the strongest counterargument is that three short helpers are easier to read, but it does not survive because their duplicated identity rules already disagree with resource creation.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/MgmtPermissionsV2.java:64 — [P2 confidence 100] Coupling advisory: `public ClientPermissions clients()` exposes the legacy concrete contract while returning `new ClientPermissionsV2(...)`, whose management methods at `ClientPermissionsV2.java:147–205` only `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`, so the next shared client-management call compiles against an API the V2 implementer cannot honor and must add version checks or another rejecting override; the strongest counterargument is that feature-gated callers can avoid those methods, but it does not survive because `AdminPermissions.management(...)` globally substitutes V2 behind the same return contract and no type boundary communicates the reduced capability.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P1 confidence 100] The cleanup gate `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` omits the sibling `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` flag, so when V2 alone is enabled deleting a client, role, or group skips permission cleanup and leaves orphaned authorization data; the strongest counterargument is that V2 might always imply V1, but it does not survive because all five factories at lines 40–67 dispatch solely on V2 and `isAdminPermissionsEnabled` likewise requires V2 plus the realm switch without requiring V1.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:359 — [P2 confidence 100] The only role-mapping test grants `Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE)` and never exercises the newly added `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`, so both an implementation that always denies client-scope role mapping and one that permits it without the scope pass this suite; the strongest counterargument is that the three role scopes share evaluation plumbing, but it does not survive because `canMapClientScopeRoles` is a distinct entry point and the test covers distinct positive and negative operations for the other two scopes.

docs/tasks/task-001.md:2 — [P3 confidence 100] Advisory: the entire acceptance contract is `Review the change.`, omitting the required matrix of six scopes across type-wide and per-client permissions, deny-by-default behavior, V1/V2/realm enable gates, and deletion lifecycle, so reviewers cannot establish that the Client resource type is complete; the strongest counterargument is that integration tests can serve as the specification, but it does not survive because those tests omit both `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` and the V2-only cleanup configuration identified above.

server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:226 — [P1 confidence 100] On upgrade, an existing V2-enabled realm already has `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so `if (client != null) { return; }` skips reconciling its persisted authorization server with the newly declared `CLIENTS` schema at line 68, leaving the `Clients` aggregate resource and the `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, and `map-roles-composite` scopes absent and making creation of those client permissions fail with `Scope [...] does not exist.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P1 confidence 100] `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` guards deletion cleanup with the V1 flag even though V2 selection and schema activation use `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, so deleting a role, client, or group in a V2-only deployment skips `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` and leaves orphaned authorization resources and policies.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — [P1 confidence 100] `Resource resource =  resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId());` supplies the resource-server ID as owner although `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` at `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` stored per-client resources under the admin-permissions client ID, so every per-client authorization check misses its resource and client-specific grants are ignored and denied.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P1 confidence 100] `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` with `granted.add(resource.getName());` enumerates only the type-level `Clients` resource because per-client resources created at `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` never call `setType`, so the downstream role-mapping path receives `"Clients"` instead of real client IDs and cannot resolve or authorize the intended clients.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:149 — [P1 confidence 100] `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2");` is reached through the newly wired `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` when FGAPv2 handles a cross-client V1 token exchange with an audience, turning the authorization check into HTTP 500 and making that token-exchange path non-executable.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — [P1 confidence 100] `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())` queries owner `server.getId()` although `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` creates that per-client resource with owner `resourceServer.getClientId()`, so the trigger of any direct client API check after granting an object-scoped permission makes the affected `canManage`/`canConfigure`/`canView`/`canMap*` caller miss the resource, fall back to `Clients`, and return 403 instead of honoring the grant.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P1 confidence 100] `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` cannot enumerate per-client resources because `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` creates them without `setType`, so the trigger of listing clients under an object-scoped grant makes the affected `getClientsWithPermission` caller silently omit every granted client and return a successful but incomplete result.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:149 — [P1 confidence 100] `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")` is the implementation reached by the affected cross-client token-exchange caller after `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` is selected, so an FGAPv2 token-exchange request triggers an uncaught runtime exception and a raw HTTP 500 instead of a bounded authorization response.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P2 confidence 75] Latent-fragility advisory: `findByType(... resource -> { if (hasGrantedPermission(resource, scope)) ... })` works today only while few typed client resources exist but, when the resource-type omission is corrected and a realm accumulates many grants, the affected client-list caller triggers one synchronous `root.evaluatePermission` at line 276 per resource plus an unpaged `HashSet` of all matches; the strongest counterargument is that only permission-bearing clients create resources, but it fails because that population is unbounded and all IDs are evaluated and materialized before downstream pagination.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P2 confidence 75] The unrelated `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` wrapper changes all existing role/client/group removal semantics: when legacy FGAP is disabled after permissions exist or V2 is the selected variant, a removal event skips every `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` cleanup call and leaves stale authorization resources and policies; although the guard avoids the new `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` exception, suppressing cleanup for all three resource types is not required to add the Client schema and does not supply the missing V2 cleanup path.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:262 — [P3 confidence 100] The unreferenced `private EvaluationContext getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token)` plus its `ClientModelIdentity`/`DefaultEvaluationContext` imports is deletable token-exchange scaffolding outside the Client-schema requirement, adding a false implementation signal and maintenance surface; although retaining it anticipates token-exchange support, that support is explicitly rejected by `canExchangeTo` and `exchangeToPermission` with `UnsupportedOperationException`, so speculative scaffolding has no present caller or requirement.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:65 — [P1 confidence 100] The override `if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS)) return true; return hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` drops the inherited `isInternal(client)` denial, so an FGAPv2 principal granted all-Clients `manage` can send admin REST update or delete requests for the protected `realm-management` client and reconfigure or destroy the realm's authorization boundary; the strongest counterargument is that internal clients are administration objects, but that is precisely why `ClientPermissions.canManage` denies them before checking roles or policies and this override bypasses that guard.

services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P2 confidence 75] The new outer `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) {` suppresses `ClientRemovedEvent` authorization cleanup when the distinct V2 feature is active, leaving client-scoped resources and policies keyed by a deleted client's ID, so deleting a delegated client and later recreating or importing a client with the same supplied `ClientRepresentation.id` gives the former delegate management access and client-secret control over the replacement; the strongest counterargument is that routine creation generates a fresh UUID, but `RepresentationToModel.createClient` honors non-null representation IDs and therefore deterministic restore or import reuses the stale grant.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:359 — [P2 confidence 100] The positive role checks are not scope-isolated because `createPermission(client, myclient.getId(), clientsType, Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE), onlyMyAdminUserPolicy);` grants three capabilities before exercising only two operations, so an endpoint accidentally authorized by `CONFIGURE` or the other mapping scope still passes and the next permission-routing change can collapse least-privilege boundaries; the strongest counterargument is that the pre-grant calls prove both operations are denied by default, but it does not survive because they establish only that no scope authorizes the calls and never identify which individual scope enables each call.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:163 — [P2 confidence 100] The client-list assertions `assertThat(allClients, hasSize(1));` and `assertThat(found, not(empty()));` at line 305 never assert returned client IDs, so a broken `getClientsWithPermission`/filter path that returns the wrong singleton or only a subset of clients passes and the next enumeration refactor can silently hide or expose the wrong clients; the strongest counterargument is that adjacent direct GET/update checks exercise the intended and unintended clients, but it does not survive because those endpoint checks do not traverse or validate the distinct list-result identity path.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:76 — [P2 confidence 100] Spec-oracle advisory: `private final String clientsType = AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS.getType();` plus the production scope constants imported at lines 26–30 makes the new tests derive their request vocabulary from the implementation under test, so a misspelled Client type or scope identifier changes producer and tests together and passes, allowing the next schema edit to break the external contract unnoticed; the strongest counterargument is that the tests exercise the resulting schema end to end, but it does not survive because no assertion independently requires the literal `Clients` type and exact public scope names.

tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:174 — [P3 confidence 100] Fragile-structure advisory: after asserting only `assertThat(defaultClientScopes, not(empty()));`, the test dereferences `defaultClientScopes.get(1)`, so a legitimate fixture change from two default scopes to one fails with `IndexOutOfBoundsException` before testing authorization and forces the next default-scope change to rewrite an unrelated permission test; the strongest counterargument is that the current realm fixture supplies at least two defaults, but it does not survive because that unstated count and ordering are outside this test's authorization contract and its own assertion guarantees only one element.

goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getClientsWithPermission() at line 138 iterates over all resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE and calls hasGrantedPermission() for each one, which in turn calls root.evaluatePermission() at line 276. This is indeed an N+1 pattern where policy evaluation happens per resource. The diff shows this is new code in ClientPermissionsV2.java. However, this is a performance/scalability concern rather than a correctness bug - the code will function correctly but may have performance issues at scale. The finding is grounded in actual diff code and raises a legitimate architectural concern about the unbounded iteration pattern.

adjudication.rationale: The finding describes code duplication and suggests refactoring, but this is a style/architecture opinion rather than a concrete defect or important non-bug issue. The claim about 'identity rules already disagree with resource creation' is vague and not verifiable from the diff. The three helper methods (hasPermission with ClientModel, hasPermission with just scope, hasGrantedPermission) serve different purposes - one for specific client permissions, one for all-clients permissions, and one for checking granted permissions on a resource. While there is some code similarity, this is a design choice and the finding doesn't identify an actual bug or critical issue that would block the PR.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a design concern: MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2 which extends ClientPermissions but throws UnsupportedOperationException for many inherited methods (lines 147-205 in ClientPermissionsV2.java show methods like isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions, etc. all throwing UnsupportedOperationException). The return type is ClientPermissions (the parent class), so callers using the interface don't know these methods will fail at runtime. This is a legitimate architectural concern about API contract violation, though it's mitigated by the feature flag check in AdminPermissions.registerListener() that guards V1-specific operations. It's not a bug per se since the feature is gated, but it's a valid design/architecture concern worth noting.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P1 confidence 100] `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` guards deletion cleanup with the V1 flag even though V2 selection and schema activation use `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2`, so deleting a role, client, or group in a V2-only deployment skips `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` and leaves orphaned authorization resources and policies.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — [P1 confidence 100] `Resource resource =  resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId());` supplies the resource-server ID as owner although `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` at `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` stored per-client resources under the admin-permissions client ID, so every per-client authorization check misses its resource and client-specific grants are ignored and denied.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims there's a mismatch between how resources are created and looked up. Looking at AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104, the code uses `resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, resourceServer.getClientId())` where the third parameter is the owner. In ClientPermissionsV2.java:214, the lookup uses `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())`. However, examining the create call more carefully at line 104, it passes `resourceServer.getClientId()` as owner, and the ResourceServer's client ID would be the admin-permissions client. The findByName at line 214 passes `server.getId()` as the owner parameter. These could potentially be different values, but the finding's claim about the specific mismatch is not clearly verifiable from the diff alone. More importantly, looking at the actual flow in hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope) at line 207-230, if the resource is not found by client.getId(), it falls back to checking the type-level resource at line 218-222, which provides a fallback mechanism. The finding overstates the severity and certainty of the issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P1 confidence 100] `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, resource -> {` cannot enumerate per-client resources because `AdminPermissionsSchema.java:104` creates them without `setType`, so the trigger of listing clients under an object-scoped grant makes the affected `getClientsWithPermission` caller silently omit every granted client and return a successful but incomplete result.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in AdminPermissionsSchema.java around line 104 (in getOrCreateResource method), when creating a resource it calls `resource.setName(name)` but does NOT call `resource.setType(resourceType)`. In ClientPermissionsV2.java:138, `getClientsWithPermission` uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...)` to find client resources. adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:149 — [P1 confidence 100] `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")` is the implementation reached by the affected cross-client token-exchange caller after `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` is selected, so an FGAPv2 token-exchange request triggers an uncaught runtime exception and a raw HTTP 500 instead of a bounded authorization response.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ClientPermissionsV2 extends ClientPermissions and overrides canExchangeTo() to throw UnsupportedOperationException. Looking at the MgmtPermissionsV2 class, when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 feature is enabled, it returns ClientPermissionsV2 from clients(). The canExchangeTo method is part of the ClientPermissionEvaluator interface and is called during token exchange flows. When V2 is active and token exchange is attempted, this will throw an uncaught UnsupportedOperationException resulting in HTTP 500 instead of a proper authorization response. This is a real bug - the method should either be properly implemented or return false/throw a proper authorization exception.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:138 — [P2 confidence 75] Latent-fragility advisory: `findByType(... resource -> { if (hasGrantedPermission(resource, scope)) ... })` works today only while few typed client resources exist but, when the resource-type omission is corrected and a realm accumulates many grants, the affected client-list caller triggers one synchronous `root.evaluatePermission` at line 276 per resource plus an unpaged `HashSet` of all matches; the strongest counterargument is that only permission-bearing clients create resources, but it fails because that population is unbounded and all IDs are evaluated and materialized before downstream pagination.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real performance concern in the new ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission() method at lines 127-140. The code iterates over all resources of type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE using resourceStore.findByType(), and for each resource calls hasGrantedPermission() which performs a full permission evaluation via root.evaluatePermission(). This is O(n) permission evaluations where n is the number of client resources with permissions. The results are collected into an unbounded HashSet before any pagination. While this is a valid architectural/scalability concern for the new code, it's not a bug per se - the code will function correctly, just potentially slowly at scale. This is a legitimate non-bug review concern about the design introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P2 confidence 75] The unrelated `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` wrapper changes all existing role/client/group removal semantics: when legacy FGAP is disabled after permissions exist or V2 is the selected variant, a removal event skips every `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` cleanup call and leaves stale authorization resources and policies; although the guard avoids the new `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` exception, suppressing cleanup for all three resource types is not required to add the Client schema and does not supply the missing V2 cleanup path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the entire event handling block for RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, and GroupRemovedEvent is now wrapped inside `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`. This means when the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is disabled, none of the cleanup calls (`setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)`) will execute for any of these events. Previously, this cleanup always ran regardless of feature flags. The finding correctly identifies that this change affects cleanup behavior for all three resource types (roles, clients, groups), not just clients. Additionally, ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, so even when the feature IS enabled and V2 is used, the cleanup for clients would fail. This is a real behavioral change that could leave stale authorization data.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:65 — [P1 confidence 100] The override `if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS)) return true; return hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);` drops the inherited `isInternal(client)` denial, so an FGAPv2 principal granted all-Clients `manage` can send admin REST update or delete requests for the protected `realm-management` client and reconfigure or destroy the realm's authorization boundary; the strongest counterargument is that internal clients are administration objects, but that is precisely why `ClientPermissions.canManage` denies them before checking roles or policies and this override bypasses that guard.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that ClientPermissionsV2.canManage(ClientModel client) at line 65 overrides the parent method but drops the isInternal(client) check. Looking at the parent class ClientPermissions.canManage(ClientModel client), it first checks 'if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS)) return true;' then checks 'if (!isPermissionsEnabled(client)) return false;' and 'return hasPermission(client, MgmtPermissions.MANAGE_SCOPE);'. The isInternal() check exists in the parent's isPermissionsEnabled() method which returns false for internal clients. The V2 override bypasses this by going directly to hasPermission() without the isPermissionsEnabled() guard, potentially allowing management of internal/protected clients like realm-management if a user has the MANAGE permission granted via FGAP.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 — [P2 confidence 75] The new outer `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) {` suppresses `ClientRemovedEvent` authorization cleanup when the distinct V2 feature is active, leaving client-scoped resources and policies keyed by a deleted client's ID, so deleting a delegated client and later recreating or importing a client with the same supplied `ClientRepresentation.id` gives the former delegate management access and client-secret control over the replacement; the strongest counterargument is that routine creation generates a fresh UUID, but `RepresentationToModel.createClient` honors non-null representation IDs and therefore deterministic restore or import reuses the stale grant.

When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, the cleanup still happens. When it's disabled, there are no fine-grained permissions to clean up anyway. The finding incorrectly claims cleanup is suppressed when V2 is active, but the code shows cleanup happens when the feature is enabled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:359 — [P2 confidence 100] The positive role checks are not scope-isolated because `createPermission(client, myclient.getId(), clientsType, Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE), onlyMyAdminUserPolicy);` grants three capabilities before exercising only two operations, so an endpoint accidentally authorized by `CONFIGURE` or the other mapping scope still passes and the next permission-routing change can collapse least-privilege boundaries; the strongest counterargument is that the pre-grant calls prove both operations are denied by default, but it does not survive because they establish only that no scope authorizes the calls and never identify which individual scope enables each call.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:163 — [P2 confidence 100] The client-list assertions `assertThat(allClients, hasSize(1));` and `assertThat(found, not(empty()));` at line 305 never assert returned client IDs, so a broken `getClientsWithPermission`/filter path that returns the wrong singleton or only a subset of clients passes and the next enumeration refactor can silently hide or expose the wrong clients; the strongest counterargument is that adjacent direct GET/update checks exercise the intended and unintended clients, but it does not survive because those endpoint checks do not traverse or validate the distinct list-result identity path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:76 — [P2 confidence 100] Spec-oracle advisory: `private final String clientsType = AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS.getType();` plus the production scope constants imported at lines 26–30 makes the new tests derive their request vocabulary from the implementation under test, so a misspelled Client type or scope identifier changes producer and tests together and passes, allowing the next schema edit to break the external contract unnoticed; the strongest counterargument is that the tests exercise the resulting schema end to end, but it does not survive because no assertion independently requires the literal `Clients` type and exact public scope names.

adjudication.rationale: The finding argues that using constants from AdminPermissionsSchema in tests is problematic because schema changes would pass silently. However, this is actually a standard and desirable testing practice - tests SHOULD use the same constants as production code to ensure consistency. The tests are integration tests that verify the actual behavior of the permission system end-to-end. If the schema constants were wrong, the tests would fail because the authorization system wouldn't recognize the resource types/scopes. The finding's concern about 'misspelled Client type' is unfounded - using shared constants prevents such misspellings. This is not a real defect or important issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:174 — [P3 confidence 100] Fragile-structure advisory: after asserting only `assertThat(defaultClientScopes, not(empty()));`, the test dereferences `defaultClientScopes.get(1)`, so a legitimate fixture change from two default scopes to one fails with `IndexOutOfBoundsException` before testing authorization and forces the next default-scope change to rewrite an unrelated permission test; the strongest counterargument is that the current realm fixture supplies at least two defaults, but it does not survive because that unstated count and ordering are outside this test's authorization contract and its own assertion guarantees only one element.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for PermissionClientTest.java, the code at line 174 shows `ClientScopeRepresentation clientScopeRep = defaultClientScopes.get(1);` but this is in the context of testing that an operation should fail BEFORE permissions are granted (it's in a try block expecting ForbiddenException). The test is checking authorization behavior, not the actual client scope manipulation. The finding misreads the test structure - the `.get(1)` access is intentionally testing a forbidden operation, and if it throws IndexOutOfBoundsException instead of ForbiddenException, that would actually be a different test failure mode. However, the assertion `assertThat(defaultClientScopes, not(empty()))` appears AFTER the permission is granted, not before this `.get(1)` call. The finding conflates two different parts of the test flow.
